canberra.title: Ministers, unions rally to defend jobs code after light rail disruption
canberra.snippet: Government leaders and the union movement have united to defend the Secure Local Jobs Code after the expiration of a certificate brought ...
canberra.content:
Work is continuing on sections of light rail stage 2A despite the stumble with the Secure Local Jobs Code. Photo: ACT Government.

Government leaders and the union movement have united to defend the Secure Local Jobs Code after the expiration of a certificate brought much of one of the ACT’s biggest infrastructure projects to a halt last week.

Work was disrupted on the light rail extension to Commonwealth Park after the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) discovered interstate traffic management firm Altus Traffic Pty Ltd did not hold a current certificate and raised the matter with Infrastructure Canberra.

Without a current certificate, Altus’s subcontractor could no longer provide traffic control services on the $577 million project.

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton reiterated his call to scrap the Code, which is under review in the wake of the corruption finding in the ACT Integrity Commission’s report on the Campbell school upgrade project.

Mr Parton said it had become a vehicle for privileged access rather than a genuine safeguard for workers and local businesses.

Master Builders ACT CEO Anna Neelagama has come out in support of the Liberals’ call, declaring the code a box-ticking exercise that favoured big interstate and international firms and only added to the administrative burden of local companies.

“Local builders have no confidence that procurement in the ACT is undertaken fairly and transparently, which is backed by the Operation Kingfisher findings,” she said.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said on Monday (24 August) that only some parts of the light rail project were affected, the firm was in the process of renewing its certificate, and Canberra Metro was using alternative traffic management.

Mr Barr accused Mr Parton of playing politics, before taking a shot at the Opposition Leader’s recent text messaging antics in Estimates.

“There’s always someone who’s going to whip up the politics here, that’s Mark Parton’s job, when he’s not bored,” Mr Barr said.

“That’s what he does, but in reality, the project continues.”

Mr Barr said the purpose of the Code was to ensure that firms contracted for government work had a history of meeting their legal obligations and that the Code was checked and assessed.

“Work is continuing on the site. It is, I understand, progressing very well,” he said.

“We’ve had a pretty good run of weather over the winter, so I think everyone wants the construction completed, and I hope the matter of a renewed certificate is resolved very quickly.”

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel says the Code maintained community expectations. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Planning Minister and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel said it was critical that there was a transparent way to ensure the government engaged ethical suppliers and for the community to make complaints.

“The ACT Government wants to make sure that we meet community expectations when engaging contractors, that they’re doing the right thing by paying proper wages and conditions and superannuation,” he said.

Mr Steel warned that the Liberals’ proposal would result in the government unwittingly hiring unethical suppliers.

“I don’t think that meets community expectations,” he said.

Unions ACT president Maddy Northam said the Secure Local Jobs Code was an Australian first that kept workers safe.

Ms Northam called it an integrity measure, and without it, there would be a race to the bottom on pay and conditions.

“Abolishing the Secure Local Jobs Code would take away a really important protection for workers right here in Canberra, for our local community,” she said.

Infrastructure Canberra confirmed that the certificate expired on 19 August, and it became aware of the matter the following day.

It said a contractual notice was issued to Canberra Metro seeking confirmation of the subcontractor’s status and requesting details of measures being taken to ensure traffic management could continue.

Canberra Metro had confirmed the subcontractor had submitted documentation to seek a new Secure Local Jobs Code certificate, and that an outcome could be expected by midweek.

“Essential traffic management measures remain in place wherever required to protect the community and workers,” Infrastructure Canberra said.

“Work is continuing across parts of the project that do not require traffic management services. Work in impacted areas will recommence once an appropriately certified traffic management contractor is in place to ensure all safety requirements are met.”

Infrastructure Canberra said the issue was not expected to have a material impact on the overall project schedule or delay delivery of Light Rail Stage 2A.

There were no expected impacts to the overall cost of the project.

canberra.title: Cold case killing caused ‘intergenerational trauma’ to Irma Palasics’ family
canberra.snippet: The descendants of a grandmother killed in what became a cold case mystery have spoken about how her death reverberated through the gener...
canberra.content:
Irma Palasics (middle) was killed by Joseph Vekony (left) and Steve Fabriczy (right). Photos: ACT Policing/Supplied.

The descendants of a grandmother killed in what became a cold case mystery have spoken about how her death reverberated through the generations of her family over the decades.

At the end of a lengthy trial in the ACT Supreme Court earlier this year, 71-year-olds Steve Fabriczy and Joseph Vekony were both found guilty of manslaughter over causing Irma Palasics’ death in a 1999 invasion.

Jurors acquitted them of the more serious charge of murder.

When their sentencing began on Monday (24 August), the daughter of Irma and her husband Gregor, Elizabeth Mikita, told the court she found it almost impossible to relive what happened.

“The trauma has shaped who I am,” she said.

“[The offenders’] actions demonstrated a complete disregard for human life.

“When I look at them I do not see remorse … I see only the darkness left by the brutality of their actions.”

Irma’s grandson, John Mikita, said he had not just lost his grandmother, but the killers’ actions had also caused the “destruction” of his family.

He remembered going to see his grandfather in hospital after the home invasion, finding him battered, bruised and barely able to speak. Afterwards, his grandfather changed.

“I watched him drink himself into oblivion,” John said.

“The offenders took my grandmother’s life, but also destroyed his.”

He said when Fabriczy was finally arrested two decades after killing Irma, he and his wife had to explain his grandparents’ tragic story to his own daughters.

“For the first time, my daughters saw me cry,” he said.

“This is the reach of this crime. It did not end in 1999 – this intergenerational trauma reached into the lives of children who were not even born when it happened.

“The person I missed the most in all of this was my grandmother. I loved her beyond words.”

Another family member said he became a suspect in the police investigation because of people he had known when he was younger – and even some in his own family suspected him. This cloud hung over him for two decades.

“I’m angry that I spent 23 years being treated as a suspect, rather than being allowed to grieve as a grandson,” he said.

Irma and Gregor Palasics, pictured when they lived at Red Hill. Photo: Supplied by family.

During the trial, jurors heard two balaclava-clad intruders, whom they found to be Fabriczy and Vekony, broke into Irma’s home in McKellar on 6 November 1999 before assaulting and tying up the 72-year-old and her husband.

The intruders ransacked the home before stealing about $30,000-worth of cash and jewellery from a hidden compartment in the kitchen. They also drank from a water container and a milk bottle in the fridge, leaving their DNA behind.

Gregor managed to free himself before he found Irma, dead, face down on the carpet in the hallway, her airway full of blood.

The DNA samples left on the drink containers in the fridge could not be identified for years. But in 2020, police finally linked Fabriczy’s DNA to the milk bottle.

In September 2023, Fabriczy met an undercover police officer and admitted he had gone to the Palasics’ house with another Hungarian called “Joe” that night. However, he claimed he waited outside as a look-out.

Police then secretly obtained a DNA sample from Vekony, which was linked to the water container.

When the sentence submissions began on Monday, the court heard Vekony had cancer and had a life expectancy of about 13 to 16 months.

His barrister, Travis Jackson, noted his client had made full denials about being at the Palasics’ home and he asked for the court to take into account his client’s health issues.

Barrister Skye Jerome, appearing for Fabriczy, said there was not enough evidence to find what exactly happened inside the Palasics’ home that night.

“It involved a home invasion that went horribly wrong and ended in the death of one of the residents,” she said.

But ACT Director of Public Prosecutions deputy director Trent Hickey asked for the court to impose the maximum penalty for manslaughter.

“We say this was a case that was just short of murder,” he said.

“[The offenders] did not care about the occupants. They were too focused on their prize, which was money.

“They must have walked past her body while they were ransacking the house or leaving.”

Justice David Mossop said he would hand down his sentence on Friday (28 August).

canberra.title: Record warmth and rain force Selwyn Snow Resort to close six weeks early
canberra.snippet: Selwyn Snow Resort has ended its snow season early, following forecasts that a decent snow dump is “unlikely” after a “...
canberra.content:
Selwyn Centre – township triple chair and home run at 3:40 pm on Monday, 24 August. Image: Selwyn Snow Resort.

Selwyn Snow Resort has ended its snow season early, following forecasts that a decent snow dump is “unlikely” after a “challenging” 2026.

“It’s certainly not the way we hoped to finish the season,” they said in an email.

“Mother Nature hasn’t been kind to us this year, and following Thursday’s rain and the significant impact it had on our remaining snow cover, our Mountain Team worked tirelessly to give us every possible chance of reopening.

“Unfortunately, the temperatures we needed for snowmaking didn’t arrive, and the time has come to call it a season.”

The announcement was about six weeks earlier than the traditional end to the snow season, which usually finishes with the October long weekend.

It’s been a disappointing one so far, with much of the Alps reporting record warmth through June and July.

For Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist David Crock, it’s not a surprise that alpine communities are seeing sparse snowfall.

He pointed to limited snow, warmer temperatures and rainy weather found across the Alps in recent weeks.

“It continues to not be a good story for the snow season … We’re reaching the last few days of August, when the natural snow pack starts to melt – and there’s not much there to start with [from this season].”

He said climate change was the “number one” factor, while El Niño has been contributing to warmer temperatures across eastern Australia.

“Climate change is making things warmer, and it’s hard to get substantial snowfall in the winter … that’s a long-term trend,” he said.

“I think last season was pretty good, at least for the Victorian resorts … Getting a good season depends more and more on luck, in terms of when you get nice big snow [dumps] and cold outbreaks through the season.”

A polar blast in 2022 brought more than a metre of snow to Selwyn – a far cry from what its slopes look like today. Photo: Selwyn Snow Resort.

Jindabyne Chamber of Commerce president Olivier Kapetanakos said the slower season left small businesses struggling.

“Businesses rely on the winter period of July and August to cover their costs,” he told Region.

“June and September are well known to be for making that little extra – there is not going to be any extra this year.”

But he believes people haven’t given up hope in mountain fun, saying he’s already taking accommodation bookings for 2027 dates.

“I think this really points to the necessity for Jindabyne and the mountains to look at a year-round economy, rather than a winter economy.

“Certainly, mountainbiking plays a big part of that. Outdoor activities … become more important when you have a pretty warm winter.”

According to forecast website SnowWatch, no snowfall is expected at any of the NSW or Victorian resorts over the next 15 days.

Mr Crock said there is “no sign” of more snow arriving in the coming days, labelling a larger dump of September snow “unlikely”.

“It’s pretty hard to see any sort of recovery this late in the season,” he said.

Instead, a rainy week is on the cards, with 15 to 40 millilitres of rain forecast for Perisher alone.

“This week doesn’t make for good reading for snowfall or snowmaking… It doesn’t look like there’s any big snow-producing systems in the next seven to 10 days.”

He warned this could result in severe thunderstorms developing.

In their statement, a Selwyn spokesperson said people with bookings for the rest of the 2026 season have been contacted.

canberra.title: Canberra’s public sonographers walking off the job every week to secure new pay offer
canberra.snippet: Unionised sonographers at The Canberra Hospital and North Canberra Hospital will walk off the job for a day every single week until they ...
canberra.content:
Public sector sonographers will walk off work one day a week, alongside other forms of protected industrial action, until they secure a better pay offer from the ACT Government. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Unionised sonographers at The Canberra Hospital and North Canberra Hospital will walk off the job for a day every single week until they can secure a new pay offer.

The ACT Government has offered a 3 per cent pay increase each year for 3 years (totalling 9 per cent) with percentage increases payable twice a year. Superannuation contributions would be increased to 13 per cent by 1 January 2028.

An additional $600 cost-of-living payment would be paid where the ACT’s annual CPI reaches 3.5 per cent or higher. The payment increases to $1000 when that figure reaches 4 per cent or higher.

Unlike other public sector workers, sonographers have called for an immediate 15 per cent pay increase.

“Sonographers across Canberra Health Services have taken today [24 August] as a strike day, and they don’t do this lightly,” CPSU regional secretary Maddy Northam said.

“Months and months and months have passed since they tabled their pay claim, and the government has come back with barely anything.

“It’s not good enough, and [sonographers] will keep doing this every week until the Barr government comes back to the table with an offer that will actually attract and, really importantly, retain staff in the public system.”

Additional industrial action, such as a ban on data entry and answering phones, is also in effect.

Ms Northam said the public system was losing sonographers to the private system or interstate, where they could either work better hours and be paid the same or do the same job but at a much better rate.

“We need public sonographers here in Canberra – something really shocking that has transpired over the last couple of years is that parents, expecting mothers, can’t get a public scan unless they hit a certain criteria,” she said.

“That means that Canberrans are going out and paying hundreds and hundreds of dollars per scan when they’re pregnant, instead of going through the public system where it wouldn’t cost them a thing.

“This isn’t good enough, and Andrew Barr needs to step up and fix it.”

Ms Northam said the workers didn’t take this drastic industrial action lightly, but the 3 per cent offer “doesn’t even touch the sides” of helping sonographers deal with rising costs.

“These workers love their jobs, they love looking after Canberrans and making sure that they get the best possible treatment here in our public hospitals,” she said.

“But they can’t do that to the detriment of them and their families.”

Union members would be open to the 15 per cent increase being phased across three years.

The sonographer and medical imaging sector across the country is under pressure due to workforce shortages.

Ms Northam argued that more needed to be done to ensure those scarce specialist workers weren’t leaving the public sector.

“We need to retain this specialist knowledge here in Canberra Health Services, otherwise Canberrans will be expected to go to the private system where we all know they’ll be paying through the nose for the exact same scans that they could have got bulk billed at the public hospital,” she said.

“The Canberra Hospital [has] a 30 per cent vacancy rate for sonographers … they can’t fill the roles, why is that? They’re not paying them properly and they can get better pay in the private sector or interstate.

“Why would they come and work for Canberra Health Services?”

North Canberra Hospital sonographer and union delegate Jackson Monk said he and his colleagues wanted to make sure people continued to receive quality healthcare in the Territory.

They hoped that securing a pay rise for the sector would preserve access to this care in the public system in Canberra, rather than losing those skills interstate or to the private sector.

“No one is out here to harm patients, no one is out here to cut health services, I think everyone is doing what they can, but it’s just about … shining a light on some areas that we could potentially do better,” Mr Monk said.

All of the ACT’s public sonographers are unionised, and represented by either the CPSU or Health Services Union (HSU).

HSU ACT Southern NSW organiser Darren Brown confirmed their members also walked off the job on Monday (24 August).

“Our members took action while maintaining emergency cover because they care deeply about their patients, but cannot keep carrying an understaffed service indefinitely,” he said.

“People are already paying the price through longer waits for scans, delayed diagnoses and delays to their care, and it simply cannot continue.

“If Canberra wants a health system capable of meeting the needs of a growing population, it needs to invest now in attracting and keeping sonographers and other allied professionals.”

HSU delegates are meeting with Health Minister Dr Marisa Paterson on Tuesday (25 August) and have postponed further industrial action while negotiations continue.

This deal is separate from the offer that has CFMEU general service officers undertaking partial work bans on litter picking in Civic and Belconnen.

Voting on that pay offer opens on Wednesday (26 August) to the estimated 11,000 eligible public servants.

Ms Northam encouraged her fellow union members to vote no on that current offer.

“We need to get the government back to the bargaining table and put a real deal on the table that at least keeps up with the cost of living,” she said.

“It’s not too much to ask that our members, that workers across the service, can pay the rent or pay their mortgage and put food on the table for their kids.

“Across the service, even workers who aren’t on the admin agreement, [are saying] to their admin colleagues, please vote no.”

Canberra Health Services has been contacted for comment.

canberra.title: KPMG to sack hundreds of staff in wake of corruption scandal
canberra.snippet: Disgraced accountancy giant KPMG Australia is slashing its workforce by 360 employees and axing 27 partners, after reporting a 1 per cent...
canberra.content:
KPMG Australia’s revenue fell 1 per cent in the 2025-26 financial year. Photo: KPMG.

Disgraced accountancy giant KPMG Australia is slashing its workforce by 360 employees and axing 27 partners, after reporting a 1 per cent revenue loss in the last financial year.

The firm will also begin consultation on a small number of award-based roles, with the overall aim of reducing its staffing levels by 5 per cent.

KPMG’s 2025-26 revenue fell from $2.278 billion the previous year to $2.257bn.

It is citing weak demand for its services, which is likely to continue beyond the next 12 months, as the reason for the move.

Some of that can be put down to the firm’s corruption in misusing confidential client information for major audits to try to win more work – compounded by the abuse of a whistleblower for raising the issue.

Since then, some large corporations have been wary of KPMG, and government work has largely been suspended, although the firm still enjoys numerous lucrative Federal Government contracts.

Ironically, the auditing arm of the business grew 11 per cent, but consultancy revenue fell 16.9 per cent over the period.

Four of the five arms of the business saw revenue grow over the financial year, but with consultancy down, most of the employees being let go will be from that arm of the company.

KPMG’s new chief executive officer John Sams said the firm had reviewed its costs and future workforce needs in response to continued economic weakness, difficult market conditions and the impact of its “conduct and whistleblower matters”.

The firm is also simplifying parts of its structure to create more connected teams and align more closely with KPMG’s global advisory services.

“This result reflects the resilience of our business and, above all, the commitment of our people in a very challenging year,” Mr Sams said in a statement.

“They continued to deliver outstanding work for more than 13,000 clients, while supporting one another through a difficult period for the firm. I am incredibly thankful for their hard work, professionalism and care.

“Our total revenue was slightly lower than last year, and below our expectations. At the same time, four of our five businesses grew, with particularly strong performances from Audit & Assurance, and Tax & Legal.

“We also continued to invest significantly in technology and build our AI capability, helping our people work more effectively and deliver better outcomes for clients.”

The CEO painted a somewhat stark outlook for the future, saying it expected difficult market conditions to continue past the current financial year.

“Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes,” he said.

“The professional services sector is also changing rapidly as client expectations evolve, AI reshapes the way services are delivered, and government spending on consultants remains lower.

“We also recognise the challenges created by our own failings, and the work we must continue to do to rebuild trust.

“While these conditions are likely to persist, we remain focused on what we can control. We will continue to monitor performance closely, act when needed and consider carefully how the firm needs to be set up for the future.”

He then announced the job cuts

“After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to reduce our workforce and restructure parts of the firm,” Mr Sams said.

“This is not a decision that has been taken lightly, and we know it will have a very real impact on people.

“With demand for consulting remaining weaker, most of the roles affected will be in our Consulting business. Changes to our business and the professional services landscape have also reduced the need for some roles in Business Services.

“Our immediate focus is on treating everyone impacted with care, dignity and respect. We are providing practical support and making wellbeing support central to the process.

“We also recognise how unsettling this will be for colleagues across the firm, and we will continue to communicate openly and support them through this period of change.”

The statement said the incoming changes were intended to put the firm on a “more sustainable footing” and ensure it remains aligned with the needs of its clients.

Several internal and external reviews will be completed in the coming months and will inform the next phase of the firm’s action plan.

KPMG has faced parliamentary inquiries since the corruption story broke, and has seen numerous executives sacked in the scandal’s continuing wake.

The firm retains a contract with the Federal Government to train rising Australian Public Service executives in leadership and integrity.

australia.title: Two men charged and drugs, guns and cars linked to CFMEU seized as police investigate alleged corruption
australia.snippet: Police arrest five men and search six properties including the union’s Victorian headquarters Get our breaking news email , free app or d...
australia.content:
Two men have been charged and Victorian police have seized drugs, guns and cars linked to the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) as part of an investigation into alleged corruption in the building industry.

On Monday, detectives from Taskforce Hawk arrested five men and searched six properties including the Victorian headquarters of the union, saying they were investigating secret commissions, fraud and drug trafficking.

Police said four CFMEU registered vehicles were seized, as well as 10 mobile phones, a Schedule 4 poison, .22 rifle and ammunition, laptops, documents, iPads and a number of USB storage devices.

No arrests were made at CFMEU headquarters, police said, and administrators for the union said none of its officials had been charged.

A 36-year-old from Chirnside Park was charged with possessing a Schedule 4 drug and bailed to appear at Ringwood magistrates court on 10 November, and a 46-year-old from Westbury was charged with failing to store a long-arm firearm and failing to store ammunition as required by the Firearms Act 1996.

He was bailed to appear at Latrobe Valley magistrates court on 11 January.

The other men were released pending further inquiries.

“The investigation in relation to the alleged secret commissions remains ongoing,” police said in a statement.

“A secret commission refers to corruptly giving, receiving or soliciting an undisclosed financial benefit, reward, payment or kickback.”

Operation Hawk was established in July 2024 to target criminal behaviour linked to the construction industry, and transitioned to Taskforce Hawk the following year.

This was in response to a number of fresh allegations of serious and violent criminal behaviour.

“Taskforce Hawk is focused on assessing new intelligence and evidence relating to allegations of criminal behaviour linked to the construction industry,” police said in a statement.

“It also continues to proactively target organised crime associated with the sector, including a focus on any individuals employed within the construction industry who have known links to outlaw motorcycle gangs.

“Police are also instigating approaches with relevant industry stakeholders to gather intelligence, as well as working closely with a range of law enforcement partners, regulators and government authorities.”

Det Acting Supt Jamie Walker, from the organised crime division, urged anyone with information, no matter how seemingly insignificant, to come forward.

“Criminal conduct, involving corruption, intimidation and violence within the construction industry is unacceptable,” he said.

“We will continue to target serious and organised crime entities and dismantle corrupt and criminal business activities in the construction industry.”

In a statement, the administrator of the CFMEU said the union was cooperating with police.

“Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector,” CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby said.

“This administration has undertaken unprecedented reform and anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future.”

The scandal was a leading contributor to the ousting of former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan, who left her post last month.

The new premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission last week.

australia.title: Australia news live: Hanson-Young says men should ‘call out’ boys’ club culture; woman dies after car crashes into Melbourne restaurant
australia.snippet: Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Alan Jones trial enters its fourth week The Alan Jo...
australia.content:
‘Shocking week for women’: Sarah Hanson-Young calls for cultural change

The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has called for Australia to confront a “culture of entitlement” that she says is contributing to “a real problem”.

Her comments follow several police investigations into sexual-assault allegations including charges being laid against students at private boys’ schools over the past week. Police in Victoria are also investigating an allegation of sexual assault linked to players in the Sydney Swans AFL team. No arrests have been made or charges laid in that matter and the players involved have reportedly denied criminal wrongdoing.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hanson-Young said:

It is quite clear that the boys’ club still rules the day in Australia.

It has been a shocking week for women right across the country.

What we need is men to actually call that out for what it is.

And I was struck by how many newspaper articles and column inches there were over the weekend from women, [who] are writing about how horrific this has been, how exhausted we all are … in the middle of this fight – and yet very little from male journalists, sports reporters, columnists, about the actual issue of men’s entitlement over women’s bodies, and the boys’ club.

We need men in this country to call out the boys’ club.

Key events

    ‘Shocking week for women’: Sarah Hanson-Young calls for cultural change

    Leah Stewart thanks community after Coogee shark bite: ‘I can finally see some light’

    Second fur seal dies of suspected bird flu

    Major housing investment near Perth aimed at increasing apartment builds

  • 11h ago

    Welcome

Melbourne council forced to combat spike in antisemitic graffiti

About 4,000 sq m of antisemitic graffiti, posters and stickers have been removed by one local council, as debate swirls around extending a royal commission, AAP reports.

City of Melbourne Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece on Monday told the commission social cohesion had frayed in Melbourne, home to Australia’s largest Jewish population, since the 7 October attack by Hamas on Israel.

A spike in antisemitic graffiti and other materials in the city prompted the council to introduce a system that allowed members of the public to report offensive material at any time of the day or night, he said.

Contractors then aim to remove the material within one hour.

Reece said 800 to 1,000 pieces of antisemitic material, covering almost 4000sq m, had been removed since the initiative started about two years ago.

SydWest Multicultural Services head Elfa Moraitakis also appeared before the commission on Monday.

Moraitakis said the Bondi attack had created unease in western Sydney’s Muslim community.

She said some Muslims, particularly women who wore a hijab, stopped going to work due to fear. Moraitakis said:

Post-Bondi, unfortunately, specific communities were used as scapegoats.

They were used as part of the political debate and this made people very uncomfortable.

Advocates and Coalition MPs have been calling for the commission, which began its final week of hearings on Monday, to be extended, saying it has not gone far enough in interrogating what led to December’s Bondi Beach attack.

CFMEU say it’s ‘cooperating fully’ with police after raids across several properties

The CFMEU and its staff say they are “cooperating fully” with Victoria police after five people were taken into custody during raids across six properties, including the union’s Melbourne headquarters.

Detectives from Taskforce Hawk executed search warrants on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged secret commissions and corruption in Victoria’s construction sector.

In a statement, administrator Michael Crosby said:

Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector.

This administration has undertaken unprecedented reform and anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future.

The CFMEU said it will also launch its own internal investigations.

The scandal was a leading contributor to the ousting of former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan. The new premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission last week.

James Paterson says Coalition immigration policy not finalised

The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, says the Coalition has not yet settled its immigration policy while speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing.

One of the reasons why is to do the work thoroughly and properly. Get it costed, get it modelled, consult stakeholders, so you don’t have four policies in four weeks like One Nation has had.

We’re going to take the time to get it right, so that by the time the next election comes around, Australians know exactly where we stand on migration and they can vote for or against us based on their judgment of that policy.

Asked whether he acknowledges there had also been inconsistency within the Coalition over immigration policy and migration numbers, Paterson said:

We haven’t settled our policy yet. And when we do, we will be behind it because we will have done the work to arrive at it.

We will have done the modelling, we’ll have done the costing, we’ll have done the consultation. It’ll be a rock-solid number that we stand behind.

Woman dies after a car crashes into shopping centre restaurant in Melbourne’s east

Police are investigating the death of a woman who was struck by a car that crashed into a restaurant at Westfield Knox in Wantirna South in Melbourne’s east.

Emergency services responded to reports of the crash at about 12.45pm on Monday, according to Ambulance Victoria.

The female customer, who has not yet been formally identified, died at the scene. A second customer was treated by paramedics at the scene.

The driver and passenger were both taken to Maroondah hospital in stable conditions.

Police have launched an investigation but said they “do not believe the incident was an intentional act”.

In a social media post, cafe Martini & Co said it was “temporarily closed until further notice”.

New Zealand to introduce bill banning social media for children under 16

The New Zealand prime minister, Christopher Luxon, said on ​Monday his party will introduce a bill in parliament that seeks ‌to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance.

The bill would require social media platforms to ​take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing ​account information, facial technology and digital identity documents.

“We simply cannot accept ⁠the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Luxon ​said in a statement, adding:

Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology ​and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.

It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient ​support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners, the New ​Zealand First party, saying it would not support it.

Read the full story here:

Nick Visser

That’s all for me! Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Have a nice Monday.

Sarah Basford Canales

One Nation described as ‘all over the shop’ with migration targets

Barnaby Joyce says his One Nation colleague David Farley misspoke when he said the party’s net migration target was “not too different” from Labor’s, describing it as a rookie mistake.

The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said the comments demonstrated One Nation was “all over the shop when it comes to migration”.

Farley, who won the seat of Farrer for Pauline Hanson’s rightwing party in May, ruffled feathers when he told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation’s net overseas migration (Nom) target was 130,000, it would allow an additional 100,000 migrant workers at a minimum. They would include skilled workers, backpackers, and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.

The final figure, of about 230,000, is slightly more than the Albanese’s government’s forecasts of 225,000 by 2027-28. Hanson insisted on Sunday that the party’s target was 130,000.

On Monday, Joyce said a mistake had been made.

Read more here:

Mar-Vic Cagurangan

US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific

A US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as the Trump administration remains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.

On Tuesday, the Marine Mineral Administration, an agency under the US department of the interior, released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28m hectares of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.

The leases ​would allow companies to ‌explore the seabed and potentially extract ‌deposits of critical minerals – known as polymetallic nodules – that could be used in batteries, electronics and defence technologies. Many environmental ​groups have ​opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.

Read more here:

Benita Kolovos

Other projects ‘more needed and urgent’ than Suburban Rail Loop, Victorian premier suggests

Continuing on from the previous post …

In an interview on ABC Radio Melbourne, host Raf Epstein pressed the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, on whether the two tunnel-boring machines in the ground in Burwood, about to begin tunnelling to Glen Waverley next month, will proceed.

Carroll replied:

The expectation is yes. The boring machines are there. There is a contract in place and that work will go ahead. But I am also having a very good look at how we fix up potholes, get on with Airport Rail, get on with Melton electrification. There are other projects that are so much more needed and urgent, and I want to make sure that Victorians know I’m governing for every corner of this state and every region of this state too.

Asked whether he will sign the contracts to build the SRL East underground train stations before the election, Carroll said he’ll have “more to say on this in the very near future”.

Epstein:

I interpret that as 100% you’re not going to build the stations. You’re delaying building the stations. Is that the right interpretation?

Carroll:

An orbital line is needed for our state, but we need to do it where it’s the best value for taxpayers … I’m not here to make any announcements on that except to say I’m having a very good look at this project, as I am all projects, to make sure we’re getting value for money. And I’ll have more to say later this week.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian premier teases update on Suburban Rail Loop

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, did the rounds on Melbourne radio this morning, suggesting he will soon provide an update on the future of the Suburban Rail Loop.

When Carroll became premier just under a month ago, he said he would be ordering a review into the costly 90km public transport project, which would also consider whether billions of dollars worth of already-signed construction contracts could be redirected.

The state government has signed about $14.5bn worth of contracts for the first stage of the loop, known as SRL East – a 26km stretch of tunnels between Cheltenham and Box Hill.

Asked by 3AW’s Tom Elliot whether he wanted to push ahead with the project, Carroll replied:

What Victorians want is a relentless focus on the basics: health, education, community safety. They do not want to be the government to be doing big, expensive projects.

They want to focus on the little things that matter so much to them. Now, on the Suburban Rail Loop, I will have more to say very soon. What I can say is … the era of ripping up contracts is over. I will stick to contracts that have been signed.

Having said that, though, Tom, I will work with the people building Suburban Rail Loop to get better value for taxpayers. The Suburban Rail Loop, an orbital line, makes sense, but it cannot be crowding out everything else we need to do as a government. Airport Rail, Melton electrification, filling potholes and doing the job properly – these are the things Victorian want from their leader and their government.

Suspended Sydney Swans players not invited to AFL’s awards night

Luca Ittimani

The AFL CEO says the five players stood down by the Sydney Swans won’t be invited to the Brownlow medal awards night.

The Brownlow medal is awarded to the best and fairest player in the AFL, awarded at the league’s annual awards night, this year on 21 September.

Andrew Dillon told reporters the invitations for the Brownlow will go out this week, but:

Those players won’t be invited … They are still eligible for the Brownlow but they’re under a club suspension which goes til the end of the season.

When their suspension is completed, the players will return to the club, he said.

Albanese maintains there will be ‘no change’ to WA’s share of GST while he is PM

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is speaking in Perth, where he said there will be “no change” to WA’s share of the GST while he is in the top job:

What I believe is very clearly there will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements while I’m prime minister. That is my view.

That has consistently been my view. The floor of 75% will absolutely stay. I think that WA deserves that. Because WA contributes to the national economy, and helps to drive that economy.

The WA premier, Roger Cook, said West Australians would be “relieved and pleased to hear the words from the prime minister today that Western Australia’s arrangements for the GST will remain”.

Cook said:

You don’t come to Western Australia on 45 occasions without appreciating that the Western Australian economy is driving the national economy. And we are very pleased that the prime minister has backed WA.

Five arrested as police raid CFMEU headquarters in Melbourne

Nino Bucci

Five people have been taken into custody after Victoria police investigating alleged union corruption raided properties including the headquarters of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) on Monday.

Police said in a statement:

Detectives from Taskforce Hawk executed warrants at six addresses this morning as part of a current investigation into information provided re secret commissions.One of the warrants was executed at a premises on Elizabeth Street in Melbourne. Five people have been taken into custody and are being interviewed by police.

Further information will be provided later this afternoon.

The Elizabeth Street property is the headquarters of the Cfmeu. Taskforce Hawk was established to investigate allegations of corruption in the construction sector after revelations of alleged graft involving the CFMEU on Victoria’s so-called Big Build.

The scandal was a leading contributor to the ousting of former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan. The new premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission last week.

AFL CEO says ‘actions of a few’ don’t define football industry amid Swans scandal

Luca Ittimani

The AFL CEO, Andrew Dillon, won’t say the game has a culture problem, saying the actions of a few Sydney Swans players don’t define the industry, after an incident that led to an allegation of sexual assault currently being investigated by Victorian police.

Separately, five Swans players have been stood down for the rest of the season for breaching club standards by “drinking … staying out late … and bringing women back to the hotel”. No one has been arrested or charged in relation to the investigation and the Guardian understands the players deny criminal wrongdoing.

Speaking to reporters in Melbourne just now, Dillon was asked if the AFL had a cultural problem. He said:

I think the actions of a few don’t define the actions of the entire industry.

He also said the league also won’t investigate the Sydney Swans incident, including hair testing for illicit substance use, until the police have finished investigating.

The players have reportedly denied using illegal drugs. Dillon said the club’s penalties were adequate and brought “accountability”.

He downplayed fan walkouts at yesterday’s Swans’ men’s game in Sydney:

Look, we saw an amazing crowd for the AFLW game, the highest crowd that the Sydney AFLW has had, over 16,000, and then we had a crowd of over 30,000 for the men’s game. There was some people that left the games in between, but that’s happened in other double headers. It was a special day for the Swans. It was a tough day.

australia.title: Dominic Perrottet’s brother allegedly shared ‘dirt’ including secret phone recording of minister, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Charles Perrottet appeared to be furthering fugitive developer Jean Nassif’s interests by undermining adversaries, a former NSW MP claims...
australia.content:
Dominic Perrottet’s brother shared “dirt” – including a secret pocket phone recording of a minister – to try to help a property developer achieve political outcomes, lawyers assisting a corruption inquiry have alleged.

Former New South Wales Liberal MP and staffer Chris Spence told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Monday that Charles Perrottet may have been acting in the interests of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif when Perrottet shared audio recordings with Spence in 2021, although he denied having knowledge of any plans Perrottet may have had at the time.

The watchdog is investigating whether Liberal figures, including the former Liberal premier’s younger brother Charles Perrottet, took donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company Toplace in exchange for outcomes, such as the removal of the former building commissioner, David Chandler, and damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott.

Spence was the MP for The Entrance between 2011 and 2015. Between 2019 and 2023, he was chief of staff between to Liberal MP Anthony Roberts, who became planning minister in 2022.

On Monday morning, Spence was asked why Charles Perrottet had shared two audio files with him in 2021, when Roberts was corrections and counter-terrorism minister.

The first, shared in May 2021, allegedly included Nassif speaking to another person about an arrangement where Chandler would give him an occupation certificate for one of his developments in exchange for a large sum of money. Charles Perrottet shared the file to Spence along with copies of text messages requesting money be paid into a bank account.

Chandler, who will appear before the inquiry later this week, is not named as a person of interest, and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

The inquiry heard the second recording – shared in October 2021 – was a phone recording taken from someone’s pocket. It purportedly included Elliott criticising Dominic Perrottet, who was then about to become premier following Gladys Berejiklian’s October 2021 resignation. Last week, Elliott gave evidence to the inquiry that Nassif began to target him after he opposed his developments, including a controversial development in Cherrybrook in northern Sydney.

On Monday, counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, asked: “Is that audio file being sent to you by Charles Perrottet not another example of Charles Perrottet ventilating dirt about Mr Nassif’s adversaries with you?”

“I don’t know that that mentions anything of Mr Nassif, but that certainly does show that yes, Charlie definitely doesn’t have a strong opinion of Mr Elliott,” said Spence.

Asked again if the files were examples of Charles Perrottet carrying out work to further Nassif’s interests, Spence said: “Upon reflection, it would look that way, but at the time, that wouldn’t have been my view.”

Spence claimed Charles Perrottet had contacted him about the alleged extortion attempt in the first message to ask him about a business near his former electorate referenced in messages. Perrottet later shared the purported recording of Elliott to ask for Spence’s help removing “background noise”, the inquiry heard.

On Monday, Spence described Charles Perrottet, who he said was a prominent member of the Liberals conservative right faction, as “very well respected, and intelligent … he was quite good at strategy”.

He rejected the suggestion the younger brother was a “conduit” to Dominic Perrottet, but said that “others would ring and complain and complain and complain, and Charlie would get frustrated not only at them, but also the fact that he just sometimes couldn’t talk to his brother.”

“There were things that the government did that he thought were silly, or that he would try and speak to his brother [about], but sometimes Dom would just be busy.”

‘Gaslit from day one’

Last week, former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos told the commission she may have been used by fellow Liberals, including longtime friend Spence and Charles Perrotet to get rid of Chandler, recounting numerous attempts in 2022 to persuade her he was “dodgy” and should be sacked. Chandler resigned in July 2022 citing concerns with Petinos, who was sacked in that month amid bullying allegations.

Petinos’ chief of staff at the time, Cassandra Lawry, gave evidence to the commission that Spence showed her a video of Chandler claiming he had provided an informal list of dodgy certifiers to banks, as well as text messages relating to the alleged extortion attempt.

On Monday, Spence admitted to showing Lawry the video, which Charles Perrottet had given him, but not the text messages. He said that Perrottet had not asked him to do anything with the video.

Asked about frequent attempts he made to contact Petinos’ office in the days before the video was published by The Australian in 2022, Spence said: “I didn’t offer them any opinion or advice. I didn’t tell them to sack Chandler. I didn’t tell them to do anything other than: ‘Here’s a topic that you need to be on top of in case you get contacted by the newspaper’.”

In its first week, the inquiry heard evidence from Dylan Whitelaw, an associate of conservative Christian factional group the Reformers, who Spence employed as a staffer in Roberts’ office in 2022.

Whitelaw described hearing Spence say he planned to give the video of Chandler to Petinos to use in a budget estimates hearing, but later came back to say: “Eleni fucked it up.”

Spence denied this had happened, describing Whitelaw as “delusional”. Earlier at Monday, he hit out at Whitelaw, describing him as “one of the most untrustworthy, lying individuals I’ve met”.

He claimed Whitelaw, who was employed by Catholic Schools NSW and a Reformer-controlled lobbying firm before becoming a ministerial staffer, “gaslit our office from day one”, and held meetings with developers by himself against office practice.

“There were periods of time when Dylan just disappeared,” said Spence.

Spence, who denied being aware of who Nassif was when Charles Perrottet sent him audio files, said he did not recall a meeting marked “Spence – Cherrybrook” in Perrottet’s diary in February 2022, or what it would have been about.

“I think our office stayed well away from [Toplace’s Cherrybrook proposal], so I don’t know what Charlie was representing,” he said.

Charles Perrottet, who has previously denied any wrongdoing, will give evidence to the commission on Friday. Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022 and is not expected to appear before the commission, has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: How do you vaccinate 1,000 tiny penguins against bird flu in the wild? It’s ‘really tricky’ but there is a way
australia.snippet: Phillip Island’s ‘iconic’ little penguins get first bird flu vaccinations in what is thought to be largest program of its kind Follow our...
australia.content:
More than 1,000 little penguins have received their first dose of bird flu vaccine in Victoria, in what is believed to be the world’s largest vaccination program involving wild birds.

Catherine Basterfield, the chief executive of Phillip Island Nature Parks, said vaccinations began early last week and were ramping up.

“This is the first time anyone around the world has attempted something like this at this scale,” she said.

“It is really tricky and penguins are difficult to handle, but we have very well trained people.

“The penguins come up the beach, they’re able to trap them in a little pen, and then move them into smaller pens to be able to then go through the vaccination administration process.”

About 5,000 birds across Phillip Island and St Kilda would receive two doses of the H5N1 vaccine, an effort that was only possible because penguins returned to the same burrows each night.

“Everybody loves little penguins,” said the state’s environment minister, Jaclyn Symes. “They’re an iconic little creature, they’re adorable, but they have a significant economic value to this region and to the state of Victoria.”

In recent nights, about 300 penguins were weighed, measured and microchipped, before being vaccinated and released. Those same birds would receive a second dose in three weeks’ time.

Little penguins are the world’s smallest species of penguin – about a ruler’s length in height – and found only in southern Australia and New Zealand. The birds, which are not listed as threatened under federal environment laws, are considered at “very high risk” from the deadly bird flu, according to a national risk assessment.

The population on Phillip Island is about 40,000 birds. The island’s “penguin parade” is a major tourist attraction, drawing about 700,000 visitors each year and contributing about $500m to the state’s economy.

The large-scale wildlife vaccination program was announced by the Victorian government on 12 August, with vaccines supplied by the federal agriculture department.

Positive bird flu cases on Phillip Island, including one in a little penguin, have increased the sense of urgency, with the team working to vaccinate as many as possible over the coming weeks.

South Australia also reported a confirmed case in a little penguin on Kangaroo Island on Sunday. On King Island in Tasmania, 51 of the animals died, with the deaths presumed to have been caused by bird flu, after one sample tested positive.

An Arthur Rylah Institute report published last year said it would take 10 weeks for penguins to reach peak immunity, and that administering vaccines after H5N1 arrived could be “too late, because significant mortality is likely to occur before adequate vaccine coverage is achieved”. In a worst-case scenario, the report said, up to 16,000 little penguins could die.

A federal agriculture spokesperson said vaccination was “one tool” that could reduce the impact on vulnerable native birds, but was “not a standalone solution”. “It does not replace effective biosecurity, which remains critical.”

James Todd, Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, said vaccines weren’t a “silver bullet”, and wouldn’t be suitable for many of the hundreds of other wild species at risk from the virus.

“In the case of little penguins, we know that they are at risk from H5, they’re a colonial species that nest together. They are a seabird that will come in contact with other seabirds that carry the virus. And we also know that they’re an iconic species that have high value to Victorians.”

Dr John Cockrem, an emeritus professor at Massey University in New Zealand, who researches little penguins, said H5 bird flu was an added threat to the species, which were already affected by severe storms, sea level rise and changes in food availability due to the climate crisis.

“So avian flu then is a threat that has arisen and comes on top of other threats that the little penguins are facing, and will increasingly face in coming years.”

world.title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says
world.snippet: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state A ⁠landslide at a huge w...
world.content:
A ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.

The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.

The death toll was 30, with six ‌people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.

Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.

One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I ‌have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.

Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite ​reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a ⁠World Bank report published in April.

On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara​, announced ​that the government was closing ​the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ​be relocated outside Conakry.

The prime ‌minister, Amadou Oury ​Bah, visited ​the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic
world.snippet: The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than...
world.content:
More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday.

The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters.

Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident. A second prosecutor from Baboua told the press that the incident is believed to have been caused by “the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating”.

“The ground completely collapsed and buried people,” Cedric Mbango, a miner at the site, told the AFP news agency, describing the incident as “catastrophic”.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident.

Grégoire Mvongo, the region’s governor told state-owned radio on Wednesday that he was “working in close collaboration with our Central African colleagues to deal with the aftermath of this tragedy”.

Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.”

The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

The Central African news website Corbeau News reported that heavy machinery, including tractors, was being used in the retrieval mission and could jeopardise the rescue of those still alive under the landmass.

The exact number of people who were in the mine at the time of the cave-in remains unknown.

Small scale artisanal mines are common in different parts of Africa, despite regulations criminalising them, as unemployment continues to drive able-bodied men to abandoned or unused mines, to eke a living. The mining sites often operate with weak safety standards leading to repeated incidents: at least 40 people have died in several mining incidents in CAR this year alone.

world.title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
world.snippet: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Seven people, including five ...
world.content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

world.title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn
world.snippet: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back The Spanish government...
world.content:
The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.

The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain and Morocco work together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”

The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.

To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.

Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.

News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.

The People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.

The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.

According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of last March 21,104 people aged 16-23 were under guardianship of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.
